topics.name: Centre of Mass: Definition, Motion, and Linear Momentum of a System of Particles
topics.summary: The centre of mass of a system is the mass-weighted average position of its particles: \(x_{cm}=\dfrac{\sum m_ix_i}{\sum m_i}\), with the same rule for the y-coordinate. It always lies closer to the heavier particles, and for two particles it divides the line joining them in the inverse ratio of the masses. For uniform symmetric bodies such as a rod, ring, disc or sphere, it sits at the geometric centre, even if no material is present there, as in a ring. The centre of mass moves as if the whole mass \(M\) were concentrated there and all external forces acted on it: \(M\vec a_{cm}=\vec F_{ext}\). The total linear momentum is \(\vec P=M\vec v_{cm}\). Internal forces cancel in pairs, so they can never change the motion of the centre of mass. That is why the fragments of an exploding shell keep their centre of mass on the original parabola, and why a man walking on a boat in still water leaves the combined centre of mass exactly where it was.
topics.worked_example:
A 1 kg particle is at \(x=0\) and a 3 kg particle is at \(x=4\) m.

\(x_{cm}=\dfrac{1(0)+3(4)}{1+3}=\dfrac{12}{4}=3\) m.

The centre of mass is 3 m from the light particle and only 1 m from the heavy one, as expected.
common_mistakes: Taking the simple midpoint or a plain average of positions instead of weighting each position by its mass.
Forgetting to divide the weighted sum by the total mass.
Letting internal forces (explosions, pushes, a man walking on a boat) move the centre of mass.
Dividing the external force by the mass of one particle instead of the total mass.
Adding momenta as plain numbers when the velocities have opposite signs or are perpendicular.

topics.name: Torque, Angular Momentum, and Equilibrium of a Rigid Body
topics.summary: Torque is the turning effect of a force: \(\vec\tau=\vec r\times\vec F\), with magnitude \(\tau=rF\sin\theta\). Only the component of the force perpendicular to the position vector matters, so a force directed along the line through the axis produces no torque at all. The direction is perpendicular to the plane of the two vectors and is fixed by the right-hand rule; reversing the order of the cross product reverses the sign. The angular momentum of a particle is \(\vec L=\vec r\times\vec p\), of magnitude \(mvr_\perp\), and \(\dfrac{d\vec L}{dt}=\vec\tau_{ext}\). Hence angular momentum is conserved whenever the net external torque is zero, even if a net external force acts, as for a planet circling the Sun. Conservation of \(L\) does not guarantee conservation of kinetic energy: a skater pulling in her arms keeps \(L\) fixed, yet \(KE=\tfrac{L^2}{2I}\) rises. A rigid body is in equilibrium only when both the net force and the net torque vanish. A couple has zero net force but a non-zero torque.
topics.worked_example:
A force of 20 N acts 2 m from the axis at \(30^\circ\) to the position vector.

\(\tau=rF\sin\theta=2\times20\times\tfrac12=20\) N m.

Using the cosine would give \(20\sqrt3\) N m, which is wrong: the cosine belongs to the work formula, not to torque.
common_mistakes: Using \(rF\cos\theta\) (the dot-product or work formula) instead of \(rF\sin\theta\).
Writing \(\vec F\times\vec r\) or using a left-hand rule, which flips the direction of the torque.
Saying angular momentum is conserved when the net external force is zero; the condition is zero net external torque.
Assuming kinetic energy is conserved whenever angular momentum is conserved.
Checking only force balance for equilibrium and forgetting torque balance, or thinking a couple produces no rotation because its forces cancel.

topics.name: Moment of Inertia: Standard Bodies, and the Parallel and Perpendicular Axes Theorems
topics.summary: The moment of inertia, \(I=\sum m_ir_i^2\), measures how strongly a body resists changes in its rotation. It depends on the mass and on how that mass is spread about the chosen axis, so the same body has different values about different axes. Standard results: ring about its central axis \(MR^2\) and about a diameter \(\tfrac12MR^2\); disc about its central axis \(\tfrac12MR^2\) and about a diameter \(\tfrac14MR^2\); solid sphere \(\tfrac25MR^2\) and hollow sphere \(\tfrac23MR^2\) about a diameter; solid cylinder about its axis \(\tfrac12MR^2\); thin rod about its centre \(\tfrac{1}{12}ML^2\) and about one end \(\tfrac13ML^2\). The parallel-axis theorem, \(I=I_{cm}+Md^2\), shifts the axis away from the centre of mass and always adds, so the value through the centre of mass is the smallest for a given direction. The perpendicular-axis theorem, \(I_z=I_x+I_y\), holds only for flat bodies lying in the \(xy\)-plane, such as a ring or a disc. It must never be used for a sphere or a solid cylinder, which are three-dimensional.
key_formulas: \(I=Mk^2\), where \(k\) is the radius of gyration
topics.worked_example:
Disc of mass 4 kg and radius 0.5 m about a tangent perpendicular to its plane.

\(I_{cm}=\tfrac12MR^2=0.5\) kg m\(^2\).

\(Md^2=4\times(0.5)^2=1\) kg m\(^2\).

\(I=0.5+1=1.5\) kg m\(^2\), larger than \(I_{cm}\) as it must be.
common_mistakes: Subtracting \(Md^2\) in the parallel-axis theorem; the theorem always adds, so \(I\) can never fall below \(I_{cm}\).
Applying the parallel-axis theorem from an axis that does not pass through the centre of mass.
Using the perpendicular-axis theorem for a solid sphere or a solid cylinder; it is valid only for flat laminae.
Mixing up coefficients, such as using the ring value for a disc or the solid-sphere value for a hollow sphere.
Forgetting to square the radius or the distance.

topics.name: Kinematics and Dynamics of Rotational Motion About a Fixed Axis
topics.summary: Rotation about a fixed axis mirrors motion along a straight line. Angular displacement \(\theta\), angular velocity \(\omega\) and angular acceleration \(\alpha\) replace \(x\), \(v\) and \(a\). For constant angular acceleration, \(\omega=\omega_0+\alpha t\), \(\theta=\omega_0t+\tfrac12\alpha t^2\) and \(\omega^2=\omega_0^2+2\alpha\theta\). A point at distance \(r\) from the axis has speed \(v=\omega r\) and tangential acceleration \(a_t=\alpha r\). Dynamics follows the same mirror: torque plays the role of force and moment of inertia the role of mass, so \(\tau=I\alpha\). The angular momentum is \(L=I\omega\), the rotational kinetic energy is \(\tfrac12I\omega^2\), the work done by a torque is \(W=\tau\theta\), and the power is \(P=\tau\omega\). When solving a problem, first find the torque about the axis (force times perpendicular lever arm), then the correct moment of inertia about that same axis, and only then apply \(\tau=I\alpha\). A larger moment of inertia means a smaller angular acceleration for the same torque. Angles must be in radians: one revolution equals \(2\pi\) rad, and revolutions per minute must be converted to rad/s before using any formula.
topics.worked_example:
A 6 N tangential force acts on the rim of a disc of mass 4 kg and radius 0.5 m.

\(\tau=FR=6\times0.5=3\) N m.

\(I=\tfrac12MR^2=0.5\) kg m\(^2\).

\(\alpha=\dfrac{\tau}{I}=6\) rad/s\(^2\).
common_mistakes: Using the force itself as the torque and forgetting the lever arm.
Using \(I\omega\) where \(\tfrac12I\omega^2\) is needed, or the reverse.
Forgetting the factor \(\tfrac12\) in \(\tfrac12\alpha t^2\), or the factor 2 in \(2\alpha\theta\).
Computing work as \(\tfrac12I(\Delta\omega)^2\) instead of the difference of the two kinetic energies.
Leaving revolutions per minute unconverted, or dividing by \(\pi\) instead of \(2\pi\).

topics.name: Rolling Motion
topics.summary: Rolling is translation of the centre of mass combined with rotation about it. When a body rolls without slipping, the point of contact is instantaneously at rest, which gives \(v_{cm}=\omega R\) and \(a_{cm}=\alpha R\). These relations hold only when there is no slipping; if a problem says the body slides, skids or spins in place, \(v\) and \(\omega\) are independent. In pure rolling the top of the wheel moves at \(2v_{cm}\) and the contact point at zero. The friction at the contact is static, never kinetic, and because its point of application does not move, it does zero work, so mechanical energy is conserved. The total kinetic energy is \(\tfrac12mv^2\left(1+\dfrac{k^2}{R^2}\right)\), where \(I=mk^2\). Down an incline, \(a=\dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1+k^2/R^2}\) and \(v^2=\dfrac{2gh}{1+k^2/R^2}\), independent of mass and radius. With \(k^2/R^2\) equal to \(\tfrac25\) for a solid sphere, \(\tfrac12\) for a disc or solid cylinder, \(\tfrac23\) for a hollow sphere and \(1\) for a ring, the solid sphere wins every race and the ring comes last.
topics.worked_example:
A solid sphere rolls without slipping from rest through a height of 7 m, with \(g=10\) m/s\(^2\).

\(mgh=\tfrac12mv^2\left(1+\tfrac25\right)\).

\(v^2=\dfrac{2\times10\times7}{1.4}=100\), so \(v=10\) m/s.

Friction is static and does no work, so no energy is lost.
common_mistakes: Forcing \(v_{cm}=\omega R\) onto a body that is stated to be slipping, skidding or spinning in place.
Treating friction in pure rolling as kinetic, \(\mu_kN\), or letting it do negative work.
Ignoring the rotational kinetic energy and using the frictionless sliding result.
Concluding that friction is zero because it does no work; it is still needed to provide the torque.
Using the wrong value of \(k^2/R^2\) for the body, or \(\cos\theta\) in place of \(\sin\theta\) on an incline.

questions.chapter_name: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

questions.question: Two particles of mass 2 kg each are placed at \(x=0\) and \(x=4\) m. Where is their centre of mass?
questions.explanation:
Use \(x_{cm}=\dfrac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{m_1+m_2}\).

\(x_{cm}=\dfrac{2(0)+2(4)}{2+2}=\dfrac{8}{4}=2\) m.

For equal masses the centre of mass is simply the midpoint.
questions.hint: Equal masses: the centre of mass sits exactly midway.
distractor_logic: Computed the sum of mass times position but forgot to divide by the total mass of 4 kg.
Simply took the position of the second particle instead of the mass-weighted average.
Divided the separation of 4 m by the total mass of 4 kg, which is not the centre-of-mass formula.

questions.question: The centre of mass of a uniform circular ring lies
options: on the rim, because all the mass of the ring is on the rim
at the midpoint of any one radius
at its geometric centre, where there is no material of the ring
nowhere, since a ring has a hole at the middle
questions.explanation:
By symmetry, every mass element of the ring has an equal element diametrically opposite.

Their contributions cancel in pairs about the centre, so the centre of mass is the geometric centre.

The centre of mass need not lie inside the material of the body.
questions.hint: Use symmetry: every bit of the ring has a partner on the opposite side.
distractor_logic: Assumes the centre of mass must be located where material exists, which is not required.
Averages the centre and the rim, which has no basis in the symmetry of the ring.
Believes a centre of mass cannot exist in empty space, but it is only a mass-weighted average position.

questions.question: For a thin uniform rod of length \(L\), the centre of mass is located
options: at a distance \(\tfrac{L}{3}\) from one end
at one end of the rod
at a distance \(\tfrac{L}{4}\) from one end
at a distance \(\tfrac{L}{2}\) from either end
questions.explanation:
A uniform rod has the same mass per unit length everywhere.

By symmetry about its midpoint, the centre of mass must be the midpoint.

So it is \(\tfrac{L}{2}\) from either end.
questions.hint: A uniform rod is symmetric about its middle.
distractor_logic: Confuses the rod with the centroid position of a triangle.
Confuses the axis often used for rotation (an end) with the centre of mass.
Halved the correct distance without any physical reason.

By definition \(M\vec v_{cm}=\sum m_i\vec v_i\).

The right-hand side is the total linear momentum of the system.

questions.question: If the net external force on a system of particles is zero, the velocity of its centre of mass
options: changes whenever the particles push on each other
questions.explanation:
\(M\vec a_{cm}=\vec F_{ext}\).

With \(\vec F_{ext}=0\), \(\vec a_{cm}=0\).

So the centre of mass moves with constant velocity (which may or may not be zero).
questions.hint: Apply Newton's second law to the centre of mass.
distractor_logic: Zero force means zero acceleration, not zero velocity; the centre of mass may be moving uniformly.
Would need a non-zero net external force to accelerate the centre of mass.
Internal forces cancel in pairs and cannot change the centre-of-mass velocity.

questions.chapter_name: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.topic: Centre of Mass: Definition, Motion, and Linear Momentum of a System of Particles
questions.question: Internal forces between the particles of a system
options: always accelerate the centre of mass toward the heaviest particle
change the total linear momentum of the system
cannot change the acceleration of the centre of mass
are always zero in a rigid body
questions.explanation:
Internal forces occur in equal and opposite pairs (Newton's third law).

Their vector sum over the whole system is zero.

Only \(\vec F_{ext}\) appears in \(M\vec a_{cm}=\vec F_{ext}\).
questions.hint: Think of Newton's third law pairs.
distractor_logic: Internal forces cancel in action-reaction pairs, so they give no net force on the system.
Only external forces can change the total momentum.
Internal forces are large in a rigid body; they just sum to zero.

questions.question: The angular momentum of a system is conserved when
options: the net external torque on it is zero
the net external force on it is zero
no internal forces act within it
its rotational kinetic energy is constant
questions.explanation:
\(\dfrac{d\vec L}{dt}=\vec\tau_{ext}\).

If \(\vec\tau_{ext}=0\), then \(\vec L\) is constant.

The condition is about external torque, not external force.
questions.hint: Look at the rotational form of Newton's second law.
distractor_logic: Zero net force conserves linear momentum; a couple has zero net force yet changes angular momentum.
Internal forces may act freely; their torques cancel in pairs.

options: only the net external force must be zero
only the net external torque must be zero
both the net external force and the net external torque must be zero
its linear momentum must be zero
questions.explanation:
Translational equilibrium needs zero net force.

options: zero net force and zero net torque
a non-zero net force and zero net torque
a net force equal to twice either force
zero net force but a non-zero net torque
questions.explanation:
The forces are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero.

moves in a straight line along the velocity at the instant of explosion

questions.explanation:
\(\vec\tau=\vec r\times\vec F=(3\hat i)\times(4\hat j)\).

questions.explanation:
\(\vec\tau=(2\hat j)\times(5\hat i)=10(\hat j\times\hat i)\).

\(d=\dfrac{60}{20}=3\) m.

questions.question: A skater spinning on smooth ice pulls her arms in close to her body. Neglecting friction, which statement is correct?
options: Both her angular momentum and her rotational kinetic energy stay constant
Her angular momentum stays constant, while her rotational kinetic energy increases
Her angular momentum increases because she spins faster
Her rotational kinetic energy decreases because her moment of inertia decreases
questions.explanation:
No external torque acts, so angular momentum is conserved.

Pulling the arms in reduces \(I\), so \(\omega\) rises to keep \(L=I\omega\) fixed.

\(KE=\tfrac{L^2}{2I}\) therefore increases; the extra energy comes from the work her muscles do.
questions.hint: Write the kinetic energy in terms of \(L\) and \(I\).
distractor_logic: Assumes energy must be conserved along with \(L\); but \(KE=\tfrac{L^2}{2I}\) rises as \(I\) falls.

questions.question: A planet moves around the Sun under the Sun's gravitational pull, a non-zero force. About the Sun, the angular momentum of the planet is

conserved, because the gravitational force has zero torque about the Sun
always zero, because the force points toward the Sun
questions.explanation:
Gravity on the planet points along \(-\vec r\) (toward the Sun).

So \(\vec\tau=\vec r\times\vec F=0\) because the vectors are anti-parallel.

Zero torque means the angular momentum about the Sun stays constant, even though the force is not zero.
questions.hint: Check the torque, not the force.
distractor_logic: Confuses the condition for linear momentum (zero force) with that for angular momentum (zero torque).
A central force has zero torque about the centre for an orbit of any shape.
Zero torque means constant angular momentum, not zero angular momentum.

questions.explanation:

questions.explanation:
The weight acts at the centre of mass: \(\tau=Mg\tfrac{L}{2}\).

About the hinge, \(I=\tfrac13ML^2\).

\(\alpha=\dfrac{\tau}{I}=\dfrac{3g}{2L}=\dfrac{30}{3}=10\) rad/s\(^2\).

\(v^2=\dfrac{2gh}{7/5}=\dfrac{140}{1.4}=100\).

Used \(k^2/R^2=1\), the ring value.

questions.question: A solid cylinder of mass 3 kg rolls without slipping down an incline of angle \(30^\circ\). Taking \(g=10\) m/s\(^2\), the static friction force on it is
questions.explanation:

Check with torque: \(fR=\tfrac12mR^2\dfrac{a}{R}\) gives \(f=\tfrac12ma=5\) N.
